title: Jacob Blesses Ephraim and Manasseh
summary: When Jacob falls ill, Joseph brings his two sons to him. Jacob recalls God's promise at Luz, adopts Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons with a full share in Israel's inheritance, and blesses them, deliberately crossing his hands to put his right hand on Ephraim, the younger. Over Joseph's protest he insists that the younger will be greater, and he promises Joseph that God will bring the family back to the land of their fathers.
story: Genesis is drawing to a close, and Jacob is putting his house in order. In Genesis 47 he made Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan; now he secures Joseph's future within the family of promise. By adopting Joseph's two Egyptian-born sons, Jacob gives Joseph a double share among the tribes, the portion normally owed to a firstborn, which Reuben forfeited (35:22; 1 Chronicles 5:1-2). The scene also repeats the pattern that has run through Genesis since Cain and Abel: God's blessing does not follow the order of birth. Jacob, who once took his brother's blessing by deceit, now gives the greater blessing to a younger son openly and on purpose. The chapter prepares for Jacob's words over all twelve sons in Genesis 49.
historical:
Luz is the old name of Bethel (28:19; 35:6), where God appeared to Jacob twice and promised him descendants and the land. Jacob's grief over Rachel's death near Ephrath, glossed by the narrator as Bethlehem (v. 7), recalls 35:16-20. A traditional site of Rachel's tomb on the road north of Bethlehem has been venerated for many centuries, although 1 Samuel 10:2 places the tomb on the border of Benjamin, which has led some to locate it farther north.

The adoption had lasting historical results. Ephraim and Manasseh became two of Israel's tribes, and because the tribe of Levi received no territory of its own, the land was still divided into twelve portions. Ephraim, as Jacob foretold, became the more prominent. Joshua was an Ephraimite (Numbers 13:8), Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom, came from Ephraim (1 Kings 11:26), and the prophets, especially Hosea, often use Ephraim as a name for the whole northern kingdom of Israel. The ridge of land Jacob gives Joseph (v. 22) is literally a shoulder, the Hebrew word shekem, almost certainly a play on the town of Shechem, where Joseph's bones were later buried (Joshua 24:32).
cultural:
Taking children onto one's knees was a gesture of acknowledgment and adoption in the ancient Near East. Rachel had wanted her maid's children born upon her knees (30:3), and Joseph's great-grandchildren would be received on his knees (50:23). Joseph removes his sons from Jacob's knees (v. 12) before the formal blessing, after Jacob has received them as his own.

The right hand symbolized strength and honor, and the firstborn expected it. Joseph positions the boys accordingly, Manasseh opposite Jacob's right hand and Ephraim opposite his left, so Jacob has to cross his arms to reverse them. The blessing formula of verse 20, “May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh”, is still spoken by Jewish parents over their sons on the eve of the Sabbath. A blessing in this world was not a pious wish but a spoken word believed to shape the future, which is why Joseph objects and Jacob refuses to change it.
literary: The chapter is full of echoes of Genesis 27. There a blind old father, Isaac, was tricked into blessing the younger son, Jacob, over the firstborn. Here Jacob is the old father, and his eyes are heavy with age (v. 10) as Isaac's were dim (27:1). But this time there is no deception. Jacob knows exactly what he is doing: “I know, my son, I know!” The verb used for his crossing of hands (see the word note) can also mean to act wisely. The younger-over-older pattern has appeared with Abel and Cain, Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Perez and Zerah (38:27-30), and Joseph and his brothers, and it will continue with David, the youngest of Jesse's sons. The blessing itself (vv. 15-16) is a short poem in three lines naming God as the one before whom the fathers walked, the one who shepherded Jacob, and the angel who redeemed him.

outline.t: Jacob recalls God's promise and adopts Joseph's sons
The crossed hands and the blessing
Jacob's promise and gift to Joseph

doctrines.note: Jacob begins with God's promise at Luz: fruitfulness, a multitude of peoples, and the land as an everlasting possession (v. 4). Everything he does in this chapter, from adopting the boys to promising a return to Canaan, is an act of faith in that covenant word.

The blessing goes to the younger because God's purposes are not bound by birth order, custom, or human expectation. Paul draws on the same pattern in the Jacob and Esau story (Romans 9:10-13). Manasseh is still blessed, but the choice of which son will be greater belongs to God.

Jacob's testimony in verses 15 and 16 is a lifetime's reading of providence. After years of flight, grief, and fear, he says God has been his shepherd all his life to this day and has redeemed him from all harm. The view is clearest at the end, looking back.

words.note: Ra'ah, to shepherd or pasture. Jacob calls God the one who has been his shepherd all his life (v. 15), the first time in the Bible that God is described this way. Jacob had been a shepherd himself for decades (31:38-40), so he knew what it meant to guard a flock through heat, cold, and danger. The image will return in 49:24 and in Psalm 23.

Ga'al, to redeem, to act as a kinsman-redeemer, the relative who buys back family land, frees a relative from slavery, or avenges a death. Verse 16 is the first use of the verb in the Bible. Jacob applies it to the angel, God's own presence, who rescued him from harm. The word later describes God redeeming Israel from Egypt (Exodus 6:6) and Boaz redeeming Ruth.

Sakal, usually to act wisely or have insight; here it describes Jacob crossing his hands (v. 14). Translators differ on whether the verb here means to cross or to guide the hands knowingly. Either way, the word hints that Jacob's gesture is deliberate, not the confusion of a blind old man.

Shekem, shoulder, and by extension a ridge or slope of land. Jacob gives Joseph one shekem above his brothers (v. 22), almost certainly a play on the town of Shechem, where Jacob had bought land (33:19) and where Joseph would be buried (Joshua 24:32).

christ: Hebrews singles out this scene as an act of faith: Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph's sons (Hebrews 11:21). The chapter's two great names for God both run toward Christ. God as shepherd becomes Jesus' own claim to be the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and God as redeemer, the kinsman who buys back what was lost, is the language the New Testament uses for Christ's work (Galatians 4:4-5; Titus 2:14). Jacob's mention of Rachel's burial near Bethlehem also finds an echo in Matthew, who applies Jeremiah's image of Rachel weeping for her children to the grief at Bethlehem after Jesus' birth (Matthew 2:18). These links are thematic, and the deepest is the pattern of grace: blessing given not by rank or right but by God's free choice, the pattern the gospel makes plain.

hard.q: Why does God keep choosing the younger over the older? Is it fair to the firstborn?
hard.a:
The pattern is too consistent in Genesis to be accidental, and the Bible treats it as a sign of grace. In the ancient world the firstborn had a natural claim to leadership and a larger inheritance. By passing over that claim again and again, the story shows that God's blessing is a gift rather than a right, and that his purposes do not depend on human systems of rank.

Christians have read the pattern in different ways. Paul uses the choice of Jacob over Esau in Romans 9 to show that God's call does not depend on works. Many in the Reformed tradition read that passage as teaching God's choice of individuals for salvation. Others read the choices in Genesis as God's selection of peoples or persons for a role in history, not a verdict on anyone's eternal destiny, and note that the passed-over son is often still blessed: Manasseh will become a people and be great (v. 19), and Esau becomes a nation too. All agree that the chapter does not despise the firstborn. It reminds every heir that what he receives from God comes from God's generosity, not his position.

questions: Jacob once stole a blessing from his blind father; now, nearly blind himself, he gives a blessing openly and knowingly. How has God reworked parts of your story that once went wrong?
After a life of struggle Jacob calls God his shepherd “all my life to this day.” Looking back, where can you see God's care that you missed at the time?
Joseph was displeased when the blessing did not follow the expected order. When have you struggled with outcomes that did not match what you thought was right or fair?
